incident.title: Checkout failing with 5xx, p99 latency above 30s
incident.alert: PagerDuty: checkout-api error rate 38% (threshold 2%) and p99 latency 31.4s (threshold 2s) for 6 minutes. Upstream: payment-service. Customer support reports card payments spinning then failing.

updates.text: Checkout failures are spreading to the mobile app; the support queue doubled in the last 5 minutes.

events.text: SEV-1 checkout failures — investigating payment-service pool exhaustion, starting with all evidence.
PR #482 moved the fraud call inside the DB transaction — now tracing how slow fraud checks held Hikari connections until the pool timed out.

args.query: Hikari pool exhaustion connection held during external HTTP call inside @Transactional

events.label: Searched runbooks "Hikari pool exhaustion connection held d" → connection-pool-exhaustion

events.text: Citation formatting was rejected — correcting the diff quote to a verbatim single line and resubmitting the full report.

evidence.supports: authorize() opens a DB transaction, saves (checking out a Hikari connection), then makes the remote fraud call before commit, so the connection is held for the whole fraud call.

evidence.quote: PR #482: Run fraud check before marking payment AUTHORIZED
evidence.supports: Trigger change: v2.14.0 / PR #482 deliberately moved the previously async fraud call into the @Transactional authorize() method.

evidence.quote: { "service": "fraud-service", "name": "POST /v1/score", "duration_ms": 7962, "status": "OK", "parent": "PaymentService.authorize", "note": "DB connection still checked out (connection held for span duration)" },
evidence.supports: During the incident a single fraud span took 7962ms while its DB connection remained checked out; DB INSERT/UPDATE/COMMIT spans were only 2-5ms.
Only 10 connections serve up to 200 Tomcat threads, and waiters fail after 30000ms - matching the 30s p99 / timeout errors.
Fraud read-timeout is 10s, so each slowed fraud call can pin a pooled connection for seconds (vs ~200ms healthy authorize).

evidence.quote: 2026-10-28T14:08:58.774Z  WARN 1 --- [nio-8080-exec-4] c.a.payments.client.FraudClient : fraud check slow orderId=ord_88241 tookMs=4120
evidence.supports: Fraud latency degraded immediately before pool saturation, rising from ~188ms to multi-second calls.

evidence.quote: 2026-10-28T14:09:12.010Z DEBUG 1 --- [l-1 housekeeper] com.zaxxer.hikari.pool.HikariPool : HikariPool-1 - Pool stats (total=10, active=10, idle=0, waiting=14)
evidence.supports: Pool fully exhausted at 14:09:12: all 10 connections active, none idle, 14 threads waiting.

evidence.quote: 2026-10-28T14:09:41.203Z ERROR 1 --- [nio-8080-exec-12] o.h.engine.jdbc.spi.SqlExceptionHelper : HikariPool-1 - Connection is not available, request timed out after 30000ms (total=10, active=10, idle=0, waiting=37)
evidence.supports: Customer-facing failure mechanism: new transactions cannot obtain a connection and time out after 30000ms, producing 5xx and 30s latency.

evidence.quote: { "service": "payment-service", "name": "HikariPool.getConnection", "duration_ms": 30000, "status": "ERROR", "parent": "PaymentService.authorize", "error": "SQLTransientConnectionException: Connection is not available, request timed out after 30000ms" }
evidence.supports: Failed checkout trace fails entirely at HikariPool.getConnection after 30000ms, before any DB work, confirming pool starvation not slow SQL.

fix.explanation: Remove @Transactional from authorize() so remote fraud/gateway calls hold no DB connection. Each paymentRepository.save() runs in Spring Data's own short repository transaction; the verdict/score is still persisted atomically with the status in the final save() call (markRejected/markAuthorized + save). The Transactional import remains used by find(). Smallest reversible change; humans should approve/apply, with rollback of v2.14.0 as immediate mitigation if needed.

next_steps: Immediate mitigation (human-approved): roll back payment-service v2.14.0 / PR #482, or deploy the proposed fix, to stop connections being held during fraud calls; do not merely enlarge the pool or scale pods (200 Tomcat threads vs 10 connections, and extra pods multiply DB connections).
Restore fraud-service capacity after its NodeNotReady event (2/4 replicas serving) and verify fraud p99 returns to ~200ms.
After the fix, watch Hikari active/idle/waiting, authorize tookMs, and checkout error rate/p99 to confirm waiting returns to 0.
Consider follow-ups: lower fraud read-timeout with a circuit breaker/fallback, enable Hikari leak-detection-threshold, and alert on pool waiting > 0.

regression_test.name: authorize_doesNotHoldTransactionDuringFraudCall

report.root_cause: Trigger -> mechanism -> impact: PR #482 (v2.14.0, deployed 2026-10-28) moved fraudClient.score() from an @Async method into the @Transactional authorize(), after paymentRepository.save(). That method therefore checks out one of only 10 Hikari connections and holds it across the remote fraud (and gateway) call until commit. When fraud-service degraded (NodeNotReady, 2/4 replicas, fraud calls rising from ~188ms to 4-8s, read-timeout 10s), average connection hold time rose ~40x, so pool throughput (10 / hold-time) collapsed: by 14:09:12 total=10 active=10 idle=0 waiting=14, then waiting grew to 66. New authorize() calls blocked in HikariPool.getConnection for the 30000ms connection-timeout and failed with CannotCreateTransactionException/SQLTransientConnectionException, causing checkout 502/5xx (38% errors) and ~31s p99.

ruled_out.reason: Incident traces show INSERT 5ms, UPDATE 4ms, COMMIT 2ms while fraud took 7962ms; failures occur at HikariPool.getConnection before any SQL. The 'payment_audit already exists' log is a benign skipping warning.
Slow requests do complete and commit (e.g. ord_88250 APPROVED in 8174ms after a 7962ms fraud call); connections are held for the fraud span duration per the trace note, not leaked permanently.
GC pauses were 18.442ms and 31.207ms, three orders of magnitude below the 30s timeouts, with heap well under 1024M.

ruled_out.hypothesis: Pool simply too small / pure traffic surge, fix by scaling
ruled_out.reason: Same pool served ~200ms authorizes at 14:03; collapse correlates with hold-time growth, not a documented traffic spike. HPA scaled 3->6 replicas and readiness still failed, and scaling multiplies held connections rather than fixing hold time.
Version-only bump with no pool/transaction change, and v2.14.0 initially served healthy 198-240ms authorizes at 14:03 before fraud slowed.

ruled_out.hypothesis: Card gateway slowness as primary cause
ruled_out.reason: Gateway call pre-existed inside authorize() and traces attribute 7962ms of an 8174ms authorize to fraud POST /v1/score; fraud slow warnings precede pool exhaustion. Gateway inside the transaction is still removed by the fix as part of the same pattern.

report.summary: PR #482 moved the fraud HTTP call inside @Transactional authorize(), so each checkout holds one of only 10 Hikari connections for the whole fraud call; when fraud-service slowed to ~8s, the pool exhausted and new checkouts timed out after 30s. Move fraud/gateway calls outside the DB transaction (or roll back v2.14.0 now).

timeline.event: PR #482 committed (tag v2.14.0): fraud check moved into @Transactional authorize() to persist verdict atomically with payment status.
payment-service v2.14.0 starts; HikariPool-1 start completed.
Healthy checkout: authorize completes in 212-214ms, fraud span 188ms.
fraud-service node NodeNotReady, pods rescheduled with 2/4 replicas serving; fraud calls slow to 4120ms, then 7311ms and 7894ms.
Hikari pool saturated: total=10, active=10, idle=0, waiting=14.
First connection-timeout errors after 30000ms (waiting=37); failed checkout trace shows 30027ms / 502 from payment-service. Alert: 38% errors, p99 31.4s.
Pool waiting grows to 52, 61, then 66 despite HPA scaling to 5 then 6 replicas; readiness probe fails.
